5: Intramuscular adrenaline (epinephrine) in the mid‑outer thigh — First‑line drug; reverses vasodilation, bronchoconstriction, and mucosal edema
Adrenaline – repeat IM dose every 5–15 min if symptoms persist; consider IV infusion for refractory cases under cardiac monitoring.

qs.q: A patient with a bleeding gastric ulcer is undergoing endoscopic injection therapy with a vasoconstrictor. What is the standard concentration and volume strategy for adrenaline injection according to the note?
qs.e: Adrenaline 1:10,000 in 0.5 to 1 mL aliquots causes vasoconstriction and tamponade and is recommended for injection therapy, ideally combined with another method.
qs.s: Upper Gastrointestinal Bleeding: Peptic Ulcer and Variceal Bleeding: MCQs

qs.q: Which specific G-protein subtype is initially activated upon adrenaline binding to its G-protein-coupled receptor?
qs.e: Adrenaline binding to its GPCR activates the Gs subtype of G-proteins. The Gi subtype is typically inhibitory and is not involved in this specific step.
qs.s: Receptors and Growth Hormone Signaling: MCQs

qs.q: A 42-year-old man presents with episodic headaches, excessive sweating, and palpitations associated with severe hypertension. Further evaluation confirms a catecholamine-secreting tumour located in the adrenal medulla. Which key enzyme is responsible for converting noradrenaline to adrenaline specifically within this tissue?
qs.e: Phenylethanolamine N-methyltransferase is the key enzyme that converts noradrenaline to adrenaline and is found exclusively in the adrenal medulla. Tyrosine hydroxylase catalyses the rate-limiting step earlier in catecholamine biosynthesis.

ai.title: Adrenaline in Clinical Practice
ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Adrenaline (epinephrine) is the first‑line drug for anaphylaxis and severe asthma. In low‑resource settings, IM injection into the anterolateral thigh is the safest route. Recognise red flags, monitor haemodynamics, and combine with antihistamines and steroids.

sections.p: Adrenaline is a catecholamine produced by the adrenal medulla that acts on alpha‑ and beta‑adrenergic receptors. It is the drug of choice for anaphylaxis and severe bronchospasm.
b: Used for anaphylaxis, severe asthma, cardiac arrest (shock), and as a vasopressor in septic shock

sections.p: Anaphylaxis is staged by the presence of skin, respiratory, cardiovascular, or gastrointestinal symptoms. Severe cases have hypotension, bronchospasm, or loss of consciousness.
In East Africa, common triggers are insect stings, food allergens (nuts, shellfish), latex, and certain medications.
Patients may have hives, angioedema, wheeze, throat tightness, hypotension, tachycardia, and altered mental status.
In low‑resource settings, clinical assessment is paramount. When available, check pulse oximetry, capillary refill, and basic labs.

t.b: Assess oxygen saturation; <90% indicates severe hypoxaemia
Look for eosinophilia in chronic allergic disease (not diagnostic of anaphylaxis)

sections.p: Cardiac arrhythmias, myocardial infarction, pulmonary oedema, and cerebral hypoxia are life‑threatening complications.
Treat the trigger, give IM adrenaline, antihistamines, steroids, and oxygen. Monitor vitals and repeat adrenaline if symptoms persist.
b: Avoid IV adrenaline unless cardiac monitoring is available

sections.p: Educate patients on avoiding known allergens, carry an adrenaline auto‑injector, and review for secondary causes of anaphylaxis.
b: Arrange allergy testing if resources allow

sections.p: Severe asthma, septic shock, and vasovagal syncope can mimic anaphylaxis but lack the rapid onset of skin and airway symptoms.
b: Vasovagal syncope – sudden fainting without wheeze or hives

sections.p: Normal eosinophil count does not exclude anaphylaxis; pulse oximetry may be falsely normal if patient is hyperventilating.
b: Oxygen saturation may stay >90% until late in shock

whenToSeekHelp: Severe hypotension, loss of consciousness, ongoing wheeze despite treatment, chest pain, or any sign of cardiac arrhythmia

faq.q: Why is IM adrenaline preferred over IV in most settings?
faq.a: IM injection is faster, safer, and does not require cardiac monitoring, reducing the risk of arrhythmias.
No; it bronchodilates via beta‑2 receptors and improves airway tone.

exam: How would you differentiate anaphylaxis from severe asthma? — Look for hives/angioedema and rapid onset after exposure.
You have a patient with hypotension and wheeze but no skin signs. What is your next step? — Consider septic shock or vasovagal syncope; obtain blood cultures, ECG, and start fluids.
In a low‑resource setting, the patient has anaphylaxis but no oxygen. What do you do? — Give IM adrenaline, antihistamine, steroids, and start IV fluids; arrange transfer if possible.
Why is IV adrenaline avoided unless monitored? — It can cause life‑threatening arrhythmias and hypertension if not carefully titrated.
What is the role of steroids in anaphylaxis? — They prevent late‑phase reactions and reduce risk of biphasic response.
